title: Characterization of triclosan tolerance mechanisms across Pseudomonas strains
abstract: The widespread use of triclosan as an antimicrobial agent has led to its dissemination in indoor and outdoor environments. Its presence may select for triclosan tolerance in members of resident microbial communities, including enrichment of the genus Pseudomonas, thereby encompassing potential pathogens. Antimicrobial resistance in Pseudomonas could negatively impact human health outcomes. However, triclosan tolerance mechanisms are not well characterized for Pseudomonas species beyond the well-studied P. aeruginosa. To elucidate the contributions of triclosan-refractory enoyl-acyl carrier protein reductases (ENR) and multidrug efflux in conferring tolerance, Pseudomonas isolates representing multiple strains from indoor dust and hospital sink drains were subjected to transposon mutagenesis and minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) testing for triclosan. A bimodal distribution of high MIC (≥128 mg/L) and low MIC (≤0.5 mg/L) isolates reflected the presence or absence of the FabV isozyme of the ENR, respectively. Among fabV-negative transposon mutants, transposon insertion increased the MIC by upregulating efflux or increasing expression of the FabI isozyme. Among fabV-positive mutants, transposon insertion in efflux pump genes reduced the MIC. Addition of an efflux pump inhibitor reduced but did not eliminate triclosan tolerance for all isolates, further demonstrating reliance on fabV for conferring higher triclosan tolerance. This study demonstrates the universal role of efflux in conferring triclosan tolerance across Pseudomonas species and that presence of fabV predicts high triclosan tolerance. Results expand upon knowledge of triclosan tolerance mechanisms within Pseudomonas species and indicate that a single strain may not be an apt representative for the triclosan tolerance profile of an entire genus.
